messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prison Guard
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 35

# A Guard's Vigilance

Fatima has worked in corrections for thirty-seven years. She started at the women's facility when her youngest was in school, took the job seriously, and built a reputation as fair and observant—the kind of guard inmates respected because she didn't play favorites and always kept her word. Her colleagues knew her as steady, someone who could defuse tension with a quiet word before situations escalated. At sixty-eight, she was months away from retirement when the assault happened.

It was a Tuesday in March. Fatima was doing her regular rounds in the intake wing when an inmate she'd never encountered before—a woman transferred in that morning—suddenly swung a makeshift weapon at her face. The attack was fast and brutal. Fatima remembers the shock more than the pain, remembers thinking this wasn't supposed to happen to her, that she'd done everything right. The weapon—a razor blade melted into a toothbrush—caught her cheekbone and temple. She was in the hospital for three days. The wound healed, but something else didn't.

That was eight months ago. Fatima retired on schedule, as planned, but retirement hasn't felt like the freedom she imagined. She and her husband, Karim, have been married forty-three years. He's a kind man, patient with her moods, but lately she can feel the strain. She startles at unexpected sounds—the doorbell, a car backfiring, even Karim coming up behind her in the kitchen. Last week he touched her shoulder while she was chopping vegetables, and she nearly dropped the knife. The look on his face when she flinched told her he was tired of walking on eggshells.

At night, Fatima lies awake replaying the moment. She's tried everything: warm milk, meditation videos, sleeping pills. But around 2 a.m., she's back in that intake wing, and the attack is happening in slow motion. Sometimes she wakes with her heart hammering so hard she thinks something is wrong with her heart. Karim sleeps in the guest room now. She told him it was to avoid disturbing him, but they both know it's because she doesn't want him near her when the nightmares come.

The scar on her face has faded to a thin line, but Fatima avoids mirrors. When she does catch her reflection, she feels a flash of rage that surprises her. She's never been an angry person, but now anger sits in her chest like something alive. She's angry at the inmate, angry at the system that brought that woman to her facility, angry at herself for not seeing it coming. Most of all, she's angry that thirty-seven years of careful professionalism, of doing her job right, meant nothing in the thirty seconds it took for her world to change.

Her daughter suggested therapy. Fatima resisted at first—she's not one to dwell on things—but she's running out of other options. She can't sleep. She can't enjoy the garden she and Karim spent years cultivating. She's canceled plans with friends. The retirement she worked toward feels like a punishment. She keeps thinking about going back to work, even though she knows that's not possible, even though the thought of being in that facility makes her stomach clench with dread.

Fatima sits in the therapist's office and describes all this in measured tones, the same controlled voice she used for thirty-seven years to maintain order. But her hands betray her—they tremble slightly as she speaks, and she keeps touching the scar on her cheekbone, her fingers finding it again and again, as if checking to make sure it's still there.
